item.title: Unruly Psychedelics
item.description:
Psychedelics

Unruly Psychedelics

Who's vying for pieces of the psychedelic pie?

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Who wants to control the growing market for psychedelics?
  • Tripping is an experience that is unpredictable, but also one that is consequential existentially.
  • Unruly psychedelics will contribute powerful and mysterious energies to the cultural changes ahead.

The value of psychedelics has skyrocketed, a shift in popular attitudes over the last few decades that is profound. Like other mind-altering substances, psychedelics satiate the human appetite for intoxication, though it seems there is much more at stake with a hallucinogenic trip than, say, getting amped up on coffee.

Who wants to control the growing psychedelic marketplace? The current administration recently exerted its control with executive orders and expanding access. Psychiatrists, clinicians, and therapists are exerting their own control in research trials and treatment protocols. Pharmaceutical companies would like control of psychedelic manufacturing, branding, and supply chains.

More liberal members within religious traditions are seeking a stake in this drug bonanza too, drawing on the New Testament, the Hebrew Bible, or the teachings of the Buddha to help interpret spiritual journeys and revitalize communities. The religious right is enamored with these substances as well, especially ibogaine, a plant indigenous to Africa, and sees them as drugging agents that can heal veterans and support Christian American patriotism. And Indigenous religious cultures would like psychedelics associated with deep-rooted histories to maintain connections with native traditions rather than be crassly uprooted and commercialized by the forces of capitalism.

Many interested parties want a piece of the psychedelic pie and seek ways to control and regulate their incorporation into the body politic.

A "Miracle Drug?"

I explore psychedelics, and psychoactive substances generally, in my book, Sacred Drugs. My take on the current psychedelic renaissance is not as sanguine as others who are convinced of their value by the evidence of research trials for treating psychological ailments. The American penchant for hyping new, so-called miracle drugs only to find out over time that the research trials might not have been as rigorous as claimed, and that the drugs may indeed pose significant dangers to some users, is a relevant, common pattern in the history of medicine in America.

Nonetheless, socially domineering forces in society emanating from the state, the market, the clinic, and the pulpit are seeking ways to contain, control, and capitalize on these valuable, mind-altering substances. But natural and synthetically produced psychedelics will not be so easily manipulated.

Unlike other drugging agents in American society, such as cannabis, coffee, alcohol, or pharmaceuticals, psychedelics will not abide by rational expectations or logical frameworks about their impact in individual bodies. Tripping is an experience that is unpredictable, contingent, disruptive, but also an experience that is awe-inspiring, cosmos-shaking, and consequential.

Does this mean the psychedelic renaissance will be a short-lived failure? I don’t think so. But I do see so much more going on in this radical collective shift around psychedelics than therapeutic promises and economic drivers. It may be prudent to admit psychedelics cannot and should not be reduced to “medicine” in the strict, scientized sense of the word, and that their effects do not simply follow a spectrum from normal to pathological. The chemical-cosmic mysteries they activate defy explanation and predictability.

article continues after advertisement

Zones of Conflict

Why are psychedelics in society so unruly? First off, psychedelics do much more than simply alter someone’s consciousness. This class of drugging substances can produce a wide range of experiences from terrifying to euphoric, but the existential impact is not limited to the tripping experience.

The trip and its transformational after-effects do not follow any uniquely common patterns. Some of what transpires might include new life orientations, self-understanding, revelations about death, and cosmic insights. In other words, a religiously infused set of sensibilities and reflections that go beyond their immediate and measurable therapeutic benefits for specific diagnoses like PTSD.

Additionally, these religious resonances do not simply lead all trippers in a direct line to God. "God," whatever that might refer to, may or may not be present for consumers. While many assume the religious dimension is singularly associated with a common mystical component that occurs during the trip, spiritual elements are spread across the entirety of the psychedelic interaction, from preparing to take a dose to living in the aftermath of its consumption.

What is remarkable today are the number of ideologies beyond institutional religions seeking to guide individuals in their psychedelic journey. The religious right would like to achieve shamanic authority over the trips of veterans and others and steer them toward righteous Christian and militaristic ideologies. The more therapeutically minded supporters of psychedelic-assisted therapy uphold Western spiritual values associated with individualism, the authority of science, and belief in an ultimately rational universe.

article continues after advertisement

Beyond the interest of conventional, institutional forms of religion to rein in psychedelic appetites, the expanding and diversifying organic networks of more free-wheeling psychedelic churches add an additional layer of spiritual contestation. These churches are seeking to answer the question all are struggling to figure out: What ultimately are we supposed to get out of these powerful hallucinogenic substances?

Of course, the entrepreneurial spirit is alive and well in the psychedelic fields, with retreats, workshops, and personal shamans available to answer the question, and each with their own rituals, myths, and morals, to offer hungry individual consumers who are suffering, discontent with life, or just looking for good times.

1960s: Return of the Repressed?

Finally, evidence for the unruliness of psychedelics is historical. Many current psychedelic enthusiasts would like to forget the not-so-distant past, but as Freud demonstrated, the return of that which is repressed comes back to haunt the individual, or a culture. The radically spiritual qualities of the cultural revolutions of the 1960s were fueled in part by the collective impact of increasing numbers of psychedelic adventurers.

The point here is that the impact psychedelics have on individual consciousnesses is only one level of impact. Whatever else you may think of the decade of the 1960s, the popularity and appeal of acid and magic mushrooms altered collective consciousness in a distinctly religious key, one that did not stop with transforming individual psychology, but opened up possibilities for social and cultural transformation. It was this spiritual power for collective action and attitudinal change in a volatile era that was most feared by Americans, and particularly government and Christian leaders who demonized and criminalized their use.

While focus is placed on the individual under the hallucinogenic influence, it’s the social and cultural reverberations of all these people tripping that will truly determine how psychedelics settle into American social life. With no head shaman to lead the way, but instead a panoply of interested parties looking to influence segments of the tripping American public, unruly psychedelics will contribute powerful, unpredictable, and mysterious energies to the cultural changes ahead.

item.title: Does Pleasure Promote Health And Bring Happiness?
item.description:
Happiness

Does Pleasure Promote Health And Bring Happiness?

Or does it lead to moral corruption and decadence?

Posted August 22, 2026

We are suspicious of pleasure. It may because the Christian tradition has often regarded pleasure as sinful, or perhaps because a person chasing pleasure is likely to neglect work and responsibilities, or because we perceive that there is an inverse correlation between pleasure and health. The author Bill Bryson famously said that the British (specifically) feel that "any pleasure involving more than a cup of milky tea and a chocolate digestive biscuit is somehow irreligiously excessive.” I argued in my book on happiness that many believe in the fallacy of a “pleasure economy,” according to which life can only be extended by renouncing and containing hedonism, just like the virtuous renounced all the dissipations of the flesh in order to access paradise in more religious times than ours. In this way, a wholesome and unpleasurable diet, in conjunction with daily, and equally unpleasurable and strenuous exercise, will earn us the right to prolong our lives, while indulging in unearned and therefore illicit pleasure (such as alcohol, fats, and sugar) will be punished with an early death.

Moral Barriers To Pleasure

Pleasurable things are good for us. In moderation, of course. We like fats and sugar precisely because our ancestors in their pre-industrial times worried about not getting enough food, a much more immediate threat to their survival than the very remote possibility of acquiring obesity-induced diabetes. The reason why we like sex is even more obvious: reproduction is a crucial requirement of life, so it needs to be rewarded with generous helpings of pleasure. However, every society and culture has felt the need to tame sexual desires with the issuing of moral rules, in order to avoid social chaos. As far as eating is concerned, nature—unfortunately—didn't expect us to be able to have an unlimited access to food, and so overdoing fats and sugars will challenge the health of a body not designed to cope with a huge calorie intake. This is why we have developed dietary rules with a semi-moral tone: the less obviously pleasurable foods (greens) are essentially good, while energy rich foods that don't even demand any work to be consumed (fast foods) are essentially bad.

But apart from the practical and functional reasons behind the moralizing of pleasure, the fact remains that many religions and philosophies see sensuality as sinful, and withdrawing from worldly carnal rewards as virtuous.

The Paradox Of Hedonism

Even before we consider the moral barriers to pleasure, we encounter the so-called “Paradox of Hedonism,” which reminds us of something that we already know, even though we may not always be fully aware of it. The paradox is that the more one seeks pleasure, the more the seeking gets in the way of acquiring it. Pleasure, some say, can only happen as a result of higher-level activities, such as altruism (that moral hue again), or otherwise by accident, when one isn't looking for it. To be fair, carnal pleasure can be reached fairly reliably, but progressing to a higher level of satisfaction is the truly elusive goal.

John Stuart Mill, the 19th-century British philosopher and liberal politician, stated that happiness was “intended pleasure, and the absence of pain” while he saw unhappiness as “pain, and the privation of pleasure.” About a hundred years earlier, Jeremy Bentham founded a philosophical approach to happiness based on the “utility” of pleasurable things, which came to be called “Utilitarianism.” Incidentally, you can still see him on the ground floor of UCL’s Student Centre in London, inside a glass case. The case contains his bones, dressed in Bentham's clothes.

article continues after advertisement

Sigmund Freud also considered the importance of pleasure. In Freud's hierarchical layers of the psyche, the "id" is basic and instinctual, governed by the more sensible and grown-up psychological strata (ego and super-ego), placed above it.

Asceticism

Long before Mill and Freud, the ancient world had already considered the merits of pleasure. The Greek philosopher Epicurus has come to be associated with hedonistic decadence, but, in fact, he enjoyed simple pleasures and believed in the value of leading a moral life. He taught that humans should be good, not in order to avoid divine punishment, but because being good was more pleasant than being bad. This is a very persuasive, "utilitarian" argument. The ancient Greek inhabitants of Sybaris, in what is now Calabria in Southern Italy, were also known for their hedonistic inclinations. It is said that they invented the chamber pot, a highlight of sybarite life. However, in the end, they were taken over by other tribes, perhaps a just reckoning for a life of excess and indulgence. Sodom, in the Book of Genesis, had a comparable fate for comparable reasons.

Away from the Sybaritic life, we encounter asceticism, its opposite pole. The merits of an ascetic life, detached from shallow distractions and mundane temptations, have been celebrated over the centuries by countless philosophies and religions. From a psychological point of view, the advantages of controlling desire, often associated with frustration, while reducing the stressful complexities of a worldly existence, are easy to appreciate.

Pleasurable Cures For Melancholia

In the Middle Ages, some Muslim physicians recommended pleasurable activities (such as good food and sex) to cure melancholia, while their Christian counterparts prescribed bleedings and purges. The former would undoubtedly have been more effective clinically, even though a depressed person will find it difficult to enjoy any pleasures as much as they did before the onset of the illness. This brings us to the complex fashion in which pleasure and happiness relate to each other.

Which Comes First: Pleasure Or Happiness?

Some see pleasure as ephemeral, selfish, and shallow, and therefore bad morally, but, as we have seen, pleasure and enjoyment are good for us, as Epicurus, Utilitarian philosophers, medieval Muslim physicians, and nature, before any of them, knew well. A life devoid of enjoyment and pleasure is a life impossible to endure. Enjoyment of some sort is a necessary condition for a minimum measure of happiness, in the same way material comfort is a necessary condition for general well-being. But does pleasure actually represent the path to happiness? It will certainly help, as we discussed, but the relationship between pleasure and happiness also operates in the opposite direction of causality. Any measure of happiness (the full amount is never available to us) facilitates the enjoyment of life. Once you have somehow managed to feel happy (to some extent), perhaps helped by the gratifications that life sometimes teasingly offers us, and after overcoming the paradox of hedonism, you will then become even more adept at experiencing joys and pleasures, even those that would go unnoticed in a flatter state of mind.

article continues after advertisement

It is an extremely elusive but perfect virtuous circle.

item.title: When Paradise Becomes a Product
item.description:
Race and Ethnicity

When Paradise Becomes a Product

Personal Perspective: The psychology of consuming places, culture, and community.

Posted August 22, 2026

Source: Sam Louie

I recently had the opportunity to visit Kauai to meet my father-in-law’s side of the family. Except for him and his sister, everyone else stayed on the island after high school. He’s a third-generation Japanese American whose family’s lineage dates back to his grandparents' immigration from Okinawa to Hawaii to work on the sugar plantations.

Kauai during his childhood was much different than it is today. There was limited tourism. The beaches were rugged. There were no lifeguards, so you swam at your own risk. People lived off the land and sea. His brother loved the ocean and was an avid fisherman, bringing home fish to feed the family. They even captured turtles for food, long before turtles became an endangered species.

They grew up poor in Kapa‘a, about 10 miles north of Lihue Airport. They walked everywhere barefoot, even to school. Life was hard, and the family knew little beyond the manual labor of working on the sugar plantations for low wages.

There was also a complicated racial and class hierarchy in Hawaii. “Haole,” a Hawaiian word for foreigner, was commonly used to describe white people or those of European descent. White people generally occupied the highest levels of the social and economic order, while Portuguese immigrants often occupied an intermediary position between white elites and the largely Asian and Native Hawaiian plantation workforce. This hierarchy was closely tied to the plantation economy and its reliance on immigrant labor.

But the hierarchy didn’t stop there. Within the Japanese community, Okinawans were often viewed as being of a lower social class than mainland Japanese in Hawaii since Okinawa was annexed by Japan in 1879. The prejudice toward Okinawans was palpable and followed them to Hawaii when they arrived as contract laborers.

Over the years, much of that animosity subsided as the various plantation communities developed a shared working-class identity that also included Native Hawaiians. Despite their differences, there was a sense of generational investment in the local communities. These families fought for labor rights, put down roots, and stayed to raise generations of families.

Today, some of that tension has shifted toward mass tourism, or what is increasingly called overtourism. The issue isn’t simply that people visit Hawaii. It’s what happens when a place becomes something to be consumed and exploited. Housing that once served local residents can become investment properties. As short-term rentals take hold, neighborhoods can become fragmented and housing less affordable for the people who actually live there.

Source: Sam Louie

Quite frankly, I’ve never had to think much about these issues while traveling. But seeing my father-in-law’s modest home, the same home he grew up in and where his two younger brothers still live, made it different. Visiting the local landmarks where he attended elementary and high school made the history feel tangible.

article continues after advertisement

Kauai suddenly wasn’t just a beautiful vacation destination where I could frolic on the beach, get a tan, and drink a few mai tais. It was someone’s home. It was my father-in-law’s home. And that impacted the way I looked at the island. It also made me think about something much bigger than tourism.

Perhaps part of the problem is psychological. We live in a culture that teaches us to maximize profit. How to make more money, more investments, more "passive income." When something has value, our capitalistic instinct is, “How can I make money from this?” rather than, “Should I?”

Having the money and means to profit from something doesn’t necessarily mean we should do it. Keep in mind, this isn’t an argument against making money or owning property. It’s a question about what happens when the pursuit of financial gain becomes so normalized that we stop considering the human cost.

Source: Sam Louie

Homes become investment income so much so that the land is viewed as a commercial commodity first and foremost, with limited thought to the impact on the surrounding community, where paradise becomes a product. We should question our consumeristic and capitalistic mindset that can turn places into something to be bought and sold. Just because something can be turned into a profit doesn’t mean it has to be. Just because we have the financial freedom to turn homes into short-term rentals doesn’t mean we have to.

Can our experiences be enough instead of making paradise a product for our own gain? Can we be content to go countercultural, even when it means passing up financial gain, so others can afford to live, maintain their communities, and have a place they call home?

Maybe that is part of what it means to travel with respect and humility to the local culture and environment. For us to remember that the place we are visiting existed before we arrived and will hopefully continue long after we leave. Paradise may be something we experience, but we also need to keep in mind it's someone else's home.

item.title: Inside Edgehill’s Rise as Everyone Starts Watching
item.description:
Anxiety

Inside Edgehill’s Rise as Everyone Starts Watching

Frontman Chris Kelly on performance anxiety, self-doubt, and staying authentic.

Posted August 22, 2026

Key points
  • Edgehill frontman Chris Kelly spoke with me about the pressure of success when suddenly everyone is watching.
  • Kelly notes that success doesn’t erase self-doubt and self-criticism can be channeled into growth.
  • For emerging artists, Kelly emphasizes an “undying belief in yourself” while staying open to progress.
Chris Kelly
Source: Edgehill / Stephanie Stewart

I first discovered Edgehill when I heard "Doubletake" on Alt Nation and fell in love with the song. I soon had the privilege of meeting frontman Chris Kelly and began following the band's rise, watching them perform as they moved from intimate house shows and touring with other bands to headlining shows of their own.

Edgehill's story began in 2021, when Kelly, then a Vanderbilt freshman studying psychology, attended a student-run jam session and met guitarist Jake Zimmermann. They clicked musically, began writing together, and the first song they completed was "Shooting Glances," Edgehill's first release.

Watching them perform, I was struck by the ease between the band members, their connection with the audience, and the energy that makes live music feel intimate, communal, and impossible to recreate twice.

But looking comfortable onstage and truly feeling comfortable are two different things.

In my discussions with Kelly for my forthcoming book, Body Business: Maintaining Mental Health and Autonomy for Athletes, Performers, and Models, which explores what happens when your talent, body, identity, and livelihood become intertwined, we talked about the psychological experience behind the performance.

At the time of our conversation, Edgehill was already gaining momentum quickly. Since then, that momentum has accelerated. The Nashville alternative band's debut album, Ode to the Greyhouse, was released on February 13, 2026. Their breakout single "Doubletake" reached No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart in April. By May, the band was preparing for its first headlining tour while Kelly was already thinking about the next album.

With a growing audience comes greater visibility, and with visibility comes the unnerving awareness that more people are paying attention.

Edgehill / Chris Kelly
Source: Edgehill / Jonathan Phelps

When Being Seen Changes the Experience

Kelly loves performing and calls it his favorite part of being a musician. Yet he revealed that he could count on two hands the shows where he had felt completely present throughout.

"The idea of being perceived definitely changes everything," Kelly told me.

Onstage, he can become intensely aware of himself, his movements, and his voice. It's easy, he explained, to feel as though people have "way more of a magnifying glass" on you than they actually do, as though they can somehow see everything you're noticing about yourself.

article continues after advertisement

He describes part of his mind as calculating: I have to do this so this happens... so we're seen as this... so it's a good show.

This constant self-monitoring is one of the less visible psychological demands of performing. You can be doing something you love while simultaneously watching and evaluating yourself doing it.

Kelly describes how this can create a feeling of disconnection. When he becomes focused on a particular "way to come across" or "way to do it right," he can lose contact with his bodily cues. During live shows, when he's hyperaware of himself, he sometimes finds words more difficult to access while talking to the audience, leaving him with what he described as a "disjointed feeling."

The more he has performed, the more creative he has become in finding ways to return to himself. Before a show, if anxiety is high, he might do a five-minute meditation, focusing on feeling his feet on the ground and bringing himself back into his body.

The band also huddles before performing, talks, jokes, and supports one another. Similarly, afterward, Kelly finds that conversation helps him come down from the intensity of the stage. "That energy has to go somewhere," he explains. Talking to bandmates, listeners, or people he trusts brings him back.

Success Doesn't Necessarily Silence Self-Doubt

We often imagine confidence as the reward for success. Get the audience, the record deal, the charting song, and eventually you'll stop questioning yourself.

Kelly watches videos of his performances and listens to live recordings. Sometimes he loves doing it. Other times, he notices the bad note or the moment he wishes had gone differently. "It is a hard thing to do. I have not mastered it, for sure," he said about keeping criticism from hitting his ego.

Part of that process is actively noticing where his thoughts go and reminding himself that an imperfect performance doesn't define him. In live music, imperfection is also part of what gives a performance its soul. No two shows can ever be exactly alike.

Evolving as a musician still requires noticing what could have gone better. The work is in changing the internal narrative from I suck to I can fix that, allowing a mistake to become something to learn from rather than evidence of inadequacy.

article continues after advertisement

That's an important distinction between perfectionism and growth. Perfectionism turns mistakes into judgments about who we are. Growth allows them to remain information about what we did.

Kelly is also learning to accept the unpredictability of live performance. When something goes wrong, he tries to remember: "You're not gonna be in this moment again. Have fun with it, laugh at it."

When Your Identity Becomes Part of the Performance

The harder existential task may be separating what you create from who other people believe you are.

Kelly told me that he sometimes worries about whether "how I'm being perceived is consistent with who I think I am." He describes performing a vulnerable song as easier because once the song starts, you know where it goes. Being yourself between songs is less predictable.

Kelly wants to reach a place where he can walk onstage and "just be me in every single way.... Whenever I don't care as much, and my identity feels like it's allowed to breathe... I have a better time, and everyone has a better time."

When the pressure to meet a certain standard takes over, he leaves the stage feeling more drained. That becomes increasingly complicated as his reach grows. Songs acquire streams, rankings, comments, reviews, and expectations.

Kelly described how quickly numbers can change an artist's relationship to something they created. If a song performs well, you may suddenly think it's better than you thought. If it performs poorly, you may begin wondering whether it's simply not good. “The song hasn't changed, but your perception of it may have.”

Staying Yourself While Everyone Is Watching

When I asked Kelly what he would tell emerging performers, his answer captured the balance he is trying to maintain himself: "An undying belief in yourself," he said, "while also wanting to grow."

When you find yourself "beating yourself up" or "feeling not enough," he said, remember that making and expressing something already has value.

article continues after advertisement

As the audience gets bigger and the stakes get higher, holding onto that belief may matter even more. Success inevitably brings more eyes, more opinions, and more expectations into the room. Staying connected to why you stepped onstage in the first place may be what keeps all those watching eyes from defining who you become.
